Eric Liddell
AIR-ik LID-ul
proper noun
Eric from Old Norse, “ever-ruler” or “sole ruler”; Liddell, an English surname from a dweller in a loud valley or by the river Liddel.

Biblical Definition

Eric Liddell (1902–1945) was a Scottish sprinter, son of missionaries to China, who refused to run his strongest event at the 1924 Paris Olympics because the heats fell on the Lord’s Day. Rather than profane the Sabbath for a medal, he stepped aside, trained for the 400 metres instead, and won gold in a then-record time, declaring that God honoured those who honoured Him. He had already learned that the Lord deserved obedience above applause. At the height of athletic fame Liddell turned from the track to the mission field, returning in 1925 to China where he had been born, to teach and preach the gospel he loved. He laboured in Tianjin and later among the rural poor, never trading the cross for the comforts his celebrity might have bought. When war came, he sent his wife and children to safety and stayed at his post, and was interned by the Japanese at Weihsien camp. There, even in hunger and disease, he organised, served, taught the young, and gave away his own rations, until he died of a brain tumour in 1945 a few months before liberation. His was a life that ran a far longer race than any stadium could measure, finishing the course in faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Scottish Olympic champion who would not race on the Lord’s Day, then gave his fame to missionary labour in China, dying in a Japanese internment camp.

ERIC LIDDELL, a Scottish runner and missionary to China (1902–1945).

Refused to run the 100 metres heats at the 1924 Olympics because they fell on the Sabbath.

Won the 400 metres gold instead, in a record time, honouring the God he served.

Returned to China in 1925 as a missionary teacher and preacher.

Died in 1945 at the Weihsien internment camp, having spent himself in service to fellow prisoners.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:8 — "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."

1Sa 2:30 — "for them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed."

1Co 9:24 — "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain."

2Ti 4:7 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:"

Modern Corruption

Liddell’s Sabbath stand and his surrender of fame rebuke an age that bows the Lord’s claims to ambition and convenience.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Liddell is that obedience to God outranks every prize the world can offer. He would not run on the day the Lord set apart, and the world that mocked his scruple was answered by his victory. The fourth commandment was no relic to him but a delight.

Greater still was his choice to leave the applause of nations for the obscurity of the mission field, and finally to pour out his life for fellow captives. His example dismantles the modern idol of self-realisation; he ran to obtain an incorruptible crown, and finished his course keeping the faith.

Hebrew Roots

A Norse name meaning “ever-ruler” joined to a surname from a loud valley or the river Liddel.

expand to see more

Eric Liddell — Eric, “ever-ruler”; Liddell, dweller in a loud valley.

Born in Tianjin, China, to missionary parents of the London Missionary Society.

Nicknamed “the Flying Scotsman” for his speed.

His running style, head thrown back, became as famous as his Sabbath conviction.

His final labours at Weihsien rooted his memory in self-giving rather than in medals.

Usage

"Eric Liddell would sooner forfeit a gold medal than dishonour the Lord’s Day."

"The crowd cheered the sprinter, but Eric Liddell ran for a crown that cannot fade."

"Even starving in the camp, Eric Liddell gave his rations away and taught the children to pray."
